source.title: Applications of the Session Rating of Perceived Exertion System in Professional Rugby Union

paper.citation: Comyns, T., & Flanagan, E. P. (2013). Applications of the session rating of perceived exertion system in professional rugby union. Strength & Conditioning Journal, 35(6), 78–85. https://doi.org/10.1519/SSC.0000000000000015
paper.abstract: How can professional rugby union practitioners calculate and use session RPE, weekly training load, monotony, and strain to manage squad and individual training? Participants: No prospectively recruited sample; examples and observations come from the authors' applied work with two professional rugby teams. Sport and level: Professional rugby union. Training or return-to-play context: Preseason and in-season squad planning, taper weeks, acute-injury return to full training, and chronic-injury load management. Inclusion and exclusion boundaries: The 24-week squad example included only a "fit to play" group completing all modalities; injured or adapted-plan players were excluded from squad averages. Design: Practitioner tutorial and narrative synthesis with descriptive examples, not a controlled intervention or formal validation study. Exposure or intervention: Session RPE monitoring across rugby, strength, speed, conditioning, and competition. Comparator: Planned versus perceived load patterns, between-week trends, and individual trends relative to a fit-to-play squad average. Measurements and outcomes: Global CR-10 session RPE collected 30 minutes after training; session load equals RPE multiplied by session duration; weekly load, monotony, and strain are derived from daily values. Analysis: Descriptive calculations and visualizations from applied professional-rugby data; no inferential analysis of the displayed team examples is reported.
paper.tldr: This applied article gives a clear implementation model for session RPE in professional rugby union, including calculation, weekly visualization, return-to-training use, and common data-collection errors. The authors' professional-rugby example accumulated average weekly loads of 2,400–2,600 AU in early preseason and approximately 1,800–1,900 AU in season, including match load. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.

paper.findings: The authors' professional-rugby example accumulated average weekly loads of 2,400–2,600 AU in early preseason and approximately 1,800–1,900 AU in season, including match load. In the within-week examples, two schedules with the same absolute weekly load of 2,125 AU produced different strain; the more homogeneous schedule increased strain by approximately 30%. In planned download weeks, athletes typically accumulated 70–80% of the training load from other weeks in the same block, according to the authors' applied observations. The authors recommend recording nontraining days as zero load because omitting zeros artificially inflates calculated monotony and strain.
paper.limitations: The article is instructional and largely experience-based; the displayed rugby examples do not report sample size, uncertainty, hypothesis tests, or injury/performance outcomes. Session RPE is subjective, and stable "high raters" make absolute values unsuitable for direct player-to-player comparison; the authors favor comparing each player's trend with the squad trend. Results and thresholds from two professional rugby settings should not be treated as universal targets for other teams, competitive levels, sports, or individuals. Timing conventions, warm-up inclusion, actual versus scheduled match duration, rest-day zeros, and fit-to-play roster definitions must remain consistent to preserve longitudinal meaning. The authors conclude that session RPE should complement, rather than replace, external-load and objective internal-load monitoring.
paper.practicalImplications: Use session RPE as a low-cost longitudinal layer that integrates the athlete's perceived internal load across training modalities. Define collection and duration rules before the season, audit missing rest-day zeros, and interpret individual trends rather than borrowing the article's absolute AU values as prescriptions. In Baylor American-football work, this rugby-union example may inform workflow design but requires sport-, position-, and schedule-specific calibration.
